introduction-when-standard-objects-arent.core: Built-in objects cover generic workloads, but platforms need domain concepts (Database, Certificate, KafkaTopic). Kubernetes is extensible: CRDs add new resource types, controllers/operators give them behaviour, admission webhooks enforce or mutate objects, and aggregated API servers add fully custom APIs, all using the same API machinery, RBAC and tooling.

first_principles.problem: Teams manage databases with scripts and wikis outside Kubernetes, losing declarative workflows.

analogy.title: Adding new words to a shared language
analogy.story: Once the word exists and everyone knows what to do when they hear it, it becomes part of everyday work.
analogy.breaks: Languages evolve slowly; CRDs can be added in seconds but need careful versioning.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Databases managed like any K8s object.

check.q: What gives a CRD-defined resource its behaviour?
check.a: A controller (operator) that reconciles instances of it.

custom-resource-definitions-crds-teachin.core: A CRD registers a new resource type (group, version, kind, scope) with an OpenAPI v3 schema for validation, optional CEL validation rules, a status subresource, additional printer columns and multiple versions with conversion. Once applied, the API server stores and serves instances like built-in objects.

first_principles.problem: Custom configuration lives in ConfigMaps with no schema, validation or status.
truths: Status separates observed state from spec.
derivation: Write **openAPIV3Schema** with required fields and enums.

analogy.title: Registering a new form type with a government office
analogy.story: Once the form template exists, clerks can accept, validate and file it.
analogy.breaks: Forms rarely change format; CRD versions need conversion strategies.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: kubectl get db works; invalid sizes rejected.

code.text:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata: {name: databases.data.example.com}
spec:
  group: data.example.com
  names: {kind: Database, plural: databases, shortNames: [db]}
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    subresources: {status: {}}
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            required: [size]
            properties:
              size: {type: string, enum: [small, medium, large]}

check.q: Why enable the status subresource on a CRD?
check.a: It separates user-set spec from controller-reported status and lets status be updated independently with its own RBAC.

operators-the-human-in-the-loop.core: An operator is a controller plus CRDs that encodes the operational knowledge of a human expert (provisioning, scaling, backups, upgrades, failover) for a specific application. Users declare intent ('PostgreSQL cluster, 3 replicas, daily backups'), and the operator performs and repairs the steps continuously.

first_principles.problem: Running PostgreSQL on Kubernetes requires a DBA to manually handle failover, backups and version upgrades.

analogy.title: An expert technician who never sleeps
analogy.story: They watch the system, follow the runbook exactly and fix issues at 3 a.m.
analogy.breaks: Technicians improvise; operators only handle scenarios they were coded for.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: HA Postgres with automated failover and backups.

check.q: What distinguishes an operator from a basic controller?
check.a: It encodes application-specific operational knowledge (backups, upgrades, failover) beyond generic reconciliation.

deep-dive-level-based-triggering.core: Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered: they react to the current state (the level) rather than individual events (edges). If a controller misses events, crashes or restarts, it simply reads the full current state and reconciles again. Events from watches only signal 'something changed, re-check this object'.

first_principles.problem: An event-driven script misses one 'Pod deleted' event and never recreates the Pod.
truths: Events can be lost or duplicated.
Re-running reconciliation is safe if idempotent.

analogy.title: Checking a thermostat's temperature instead of counting clicks
analogy.story: You don't need to know how many times it changed, just what it is now.
analogy.breaks: Thermostats measure continuously; controllers reconcile when triggered or on resync.

example.title: Missed event
flow: Edge-triggered: 'delete' event lost → Pod never recreated
Level-triggered: next reconcile sees 2 of 3 Pods → creates one

check.a: So they recover from missed or duplicated events by always reconciling against current state.

building-operators-the-tech-stack.core: Operators are usually built in Go with controller-runtime, scaffolded by Kubebuilder or Operator SDK, which generate CRD manifests, RBAC, webhooks and a manager with informers, caches and work queues. Alternatives include Java Operator SDK, kopf (Python), Metacontroller and Crossplane compositions for infrastructure.

first_principles.problem: Writing informers, caches, queues and leader election from scratch is complex and error-prone.

analogy.title: A building kit with pre-made frames
analogy.story: You focus on the custom rooms, not cutting every beam.
analogy.breaks: Kits fit one design; operators must handle many failure scenarios on top.

code.text:
kubebuilder init --domain example.com --repo github.com/acme/db-operator
kubebuilder create api --group data --version v1 --kind Database
make manifests && make install && make run

check.q: Which Go library underpins Kubebuilder and Operator SDK?

webhooks-intercepting-requests.core: Admission webhooks are HTTPS services the API server calls during admission. Mutating webhooks change objects (inject sidecars, add defaults, labels); validating webhooks accept or reject (enforce policy). Configure failurePolicy, timeouts, namespace and object selectors carefully, or a down webhook can block the whole cluster. For simple rules, prefer CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy.

first_principles.problem: A broken policy webhook with failurePolicy: Fail blocks all Pod creation cluster-wide, including its own restart.
truths: Webhooks sit in the request path.
Simple rules don't need external services.
derivation: Exclude **kube-system** and the webhook's own namespace.

analogy.title: Security checkpoints in a corridor
analogy.story: Every visitor passes through; if the checkpoint closes, nobody gets through.
analogy.breaks: Checkpoints have guards to improvise; webhooks just time out or fail.

example.title: CEL policy instead of a webhook

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Policy enforced in-process, no external service to fail.

code.text:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata: {name: require-team-label}
spec:
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules: [{apiGroups: [apps], apiVersions: [v1], operations: [CREATE, UPDATE], resources: [deployments]}]
  validations:
  - expression: "has(object.metadata.labels) && 'team' in object.metadata.labels"
    message: "Deployments must have a team label"

check.q: Why exclude a webhook's own namespace from its scope?
check.a: Otherwise a failing webhook can block its own Pods from restarting, deadlocking the cluster.

aggregated-api-servers-advanced.core: API aggregation lets you register an extension API server behind the main kube-apiserver (via APIService objects). Requests for that group are proxied to your server, which can implement custom storage, non-CRUD semantics or computed resources, as metrics-server does for metrics.k8s.io. It's powerful but much more work than CRDs.

first_principles.problem: A team needs an API backed by an external database with custom query semantics that CRDs can't express.
truths: CRDs store in etcd with standard semantics.
The main API server can proxy requests.
derivation: Use **aggregation** for custom storage, subresources, computed data.
Run **HA**; outages break that API group.

analogy.title: A department store renting floor space to a specialist shop
analogy.story: Customers enter through the main store, but the specialist runs its own counter.
analogy.breaks: Customers see different branding; aggregated APIs look identical to built-in ones.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Computed metrics look like native resources.

code.text:
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
kubectl top pods   # served by metrics-server via aggregation

check.q: Which common component uses the API aggregation layer?
